title: You’re a Role Model Now (Sorry)
subtitle: Make your influence safe to learn from
summary: Pip sees colleagues copying a shortcut and an apology. Senior behavior sets standards. Ownership, communication, mentoring, and technical and ethical judgment should strengthen others’ capability. An exemplar is different from the workshop’s permanent approval queue.

concepts.title: Exemplar
concepts.body: Pip skips a review step, and next week it is the workshop’s new habit. People notice what senior engineers reward, ignore, and excuse. An exemplar makes useful standards visible and repeatable, including how to be wrong. Pip explains a rollback in the same forum as everyone else and acknowledges the mistaken assumption. That reaction can establish a stronger norm than a policy nobody sees practiced.

steps.text: Pip notices the workshop copying senior behavior.
What gets rewarded or excused becomes a signal.
Model the useful correction, including how to be wrong.

concepts.title: Ownership
concepts.body: A support gap appears between teams. Pip takes responsibility for closing it, not for personally owning every future ticket. Ownership means noticing a consequential gap, sharing context, establishing who can act, and following through on the outcome. Pip helps the teams agree responsibility and keeps the handoff visible. The workshop gains capability instead of another private collection of tasks only one expert can touch.

steps.text: The boundary leaves an outcome without an owner.
Follow through without retaining every future task.

concepts.title: Mentoring
concepts.body: A newer engineer asks Pip how to roll out safely. Pip nearly takes the keyboard, then asks the learner to propose guardrails first. Mentoring makes room for another person’s reasoning, choices, and growth. Context and support should match the stakes. If every discussion ends with Pip doing the work, the immediate patch may improve while independence does not. The learner needs practice deciding, not merely watching expertise.

steps.text: Pip leaves room for the learner’s reasoning.
The new owner proposes a safe approach.
Offer context and escalation without taking back the keyboard.

concepts.title: Bottleneck
concepts.body: The release queue pauses whenever Pip leaves the workshop. Hidden knowledge and retained approvals have made one expert the bottleneck. Delegating tasks did not help while decisions still waited at the desk. Pip shares context, builds a checklist with colleagues, and transfers real decision authority. Confidence and knowledge should let useful work continue without Pip; being indispensable to every step is not the desired result.

steps.text: Pip asks what happens during an absence.
Work waiting for one expert reveals a bottleneck.
Build authority and confidence so colleagues can proceed.

misconceptions.claim: a staff-plus role is mainly about applying a universal formula.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter treats judgment as contextual: identify forces, listen to evidence, and adapt the response to the actual system and people.

misconceptions.claim: A visible activity or artifact proves the work is complete.
misconceptions.correction: Completion requires a useful outcome, shared understanding, and a way to notice whether the decision worked over time.

scenario.title: Mentor without bottleneck
scenario.context: A newer workshop engineer owns a risky rollout. Pip can approve every change or agree guardrails and coaching check-ins.

options.label: Coach with guardrails
options.benefit: The engineer practices judgment within a clear safety boundary.
options.cost: Coaching takes patience and allows a different safe choice.
options.consequence: Pip and the owner agree guardrails and check-ins. The engineer decides; Pip stays available for escalation.

options.label: Approve every change
options.benefit: Pip sees every change before it ships.
options.cost: Independent judgment gets little room to develop.
options.consequence: The release waits on Pip’s queue. Risk feels controlled, but the important reasoning remains private and the learner stays dependent.

scenario.debrief: Pip’s help should make the next safe decision less dependent on Pip. Guardrails and shared context can build that capacity.

quiz.question: Why does a staff engineer need care when thinking aloud?
options: Others may interpret a senior person’s idea as a decision
Every statement must be a formal document
quiz.explanation: Visible senior behavior has influence beyond the speaker’s intended certainty.

quiz.question: How can taking ownership avoid creating dependency on one expert?
options: Share context and grow other decision makers
quiz.explanation: Ownership strengthens the outcome and the team’s ability to continue independently.

quiz.question: What is a warning sign that mentoring is becoming a bottleneck?
options: Progress always waits for the mentor to make the decision
quiz.explanation: Helping should build the learner’s judgment rather than retain all authority.

exercise.title: Make the next move legible
exercise.prompt: Describe a staff-level decision, the people and terrain involved, and the route by which you will learn whether it worked.

fields.label: What decision should the mentee own?
fields.placeholder: Write the concrete facts, people, and constraint.

fields.label: Which guardrail protects users?
fields.placeholder: State the choice and its trade-off.

fields.label: Where must I avoid becoming a gatekeeper?
fields.placeholder: Name the evidence or conversation that will revisit it.
